DECLARATION OF COURTNEY VEAL
IN SUPPORT OF DEFENDANTS-APPELLANTS’ 
MOTION TO EXPEDITE APPEAL AND 
MOTION TO STAY THE TRO PENDING APPEAL
I, Courtney Veal, declare as follows: 
1. I am over 18 years of age. I make this Declaration based on
my own personal knowledge and my review of records and information 
maintained by the Judicial Qualifications Commission of Georgia (the 
“Commission”).
2. I am the Director of the Commission. I have held this position
since April 2023. From March 2020 to April 2023, I served as the Commission’s Deputy Director. As Director, I supervise the Commission’s Investigative Panel staff, oversee the Commission’s daily operations, train 
and offer guidance to Georgia’s judiciary on judicial ethics, oversee the 
USCA11 Case: 26-11705 Document: 7-2 Date Filed: 05/15/2026 Page: 1 of 7 
4a

- 2- 
Commission’s official functions, and prosecute matters on behalf of the 
Commission’s Investigative Panel before the Commission’s Hearing 
Panel.
3. I make this record on personal knowledge and on the litigation record in support of (1) Appellants’ Motion to Expedite this Appeal
and (2) Appellants’ Motion to Stay the Temporary Restraining Order 
pending Appeal. 
The Commission’s Role and Rule 29 Process
4. The Georgia Constitution establishes the Commission to ensure the integrity of the State’s judiciary and protect public confidence in 
the judicial system. The Commission is charged with investigating and 
prosecuting violations of the Georgia Code of Judicial Conduct.
5. The Commission’s Investigative Panel Special Committee on 
Judicial Election Campaign Intervention (the “Special Committee”) is 
specifically tasked with dealing expeditiously with allegations of ethical 
misconduct in campaigns for judicial office during election years. The 
Special Committee’s principal election-year function is addressing alleged campaign misconduct and, where appropriate, issuing public statements to ensure voters are informed before they cast their ballots. 
USCA11 Case: 26-11705 Document: 7-2 Date Filed: 05/15/2026 Page: 2 of 7 
5a

- 3- 
6. The Special Committee’s Rule-29 process is designed to operate on an expedited basis precisely because of the time-sensitive nature 
of judicial elections. Commission Rule 29(C) directs that the extent practicable, the Special Committee must seek to complete its process within 
10 days of receiving a complaint.
The Factual Background and Timeline
7. Election Day for the Georgia Supreme Court races at issue in 
this case is May 19, 2026. Early voting began on April 27, 2026, and is 
currently ongoing. Voters are actively casting ballots in this election as 
of the date of this declaration.
8. The Special Committee issued its confidential notices to Jennifer Auer Jordan and ShaMiracle Johnson Rankin on April 27, 2026—
the same day that early voting began. The notices informed the recipients 
that the Commission had received complaints against them, that the Special Committee believed that the complaints’ allegations warranted further investigation, and asked the recipients to respond to the allegations 
set forth in the notices.
9. The confidential notices did not request that Plaintiffs change 
their behavior or to otherwise take any action other than submitting a 
USCA11 Case: 26-11705 Document: 7-2 Date Filed: 05/15/2026 Page: 3 of 7 
6a

- 4- 
confidential written response addressing the allegations. The notices did 
not request that Plaintiffs remove any postings, alter any speech, or in 
any way change any of their campaign conduct during the pendency of 
the investigation.
10. All of the speech that the Special Committee identified in its 
April 27, 2026, confidential notices remains publicly posted by Plaintiffs 
on their campaign websites and social media pages. On May 8, 2026, I 
verified that the campaign commercial, endorsement postings, and other 
campaign material referenced in the notices remained publicly available 
on Plaintiffs’ accounts. App’x 91-182. 
11. Plaintiffs, through counsel, submitted written responses to 
the Special Committee’s notices on April 30, 2026. Rather than substantively addressing the allegations, the responses informed the Commission that Plaintiffs had filed a sealed federal lawsuit earlier that day. 
Irreparable Harm and the Need for Immediate Resolution
12. The May 19, 2026, election is the only election period that 
matters for the Special Committee’s investigation of Plaintiff’s conduct. 
If the TRO remains in place through Election Day—or if this appeal is 
not resolved before then—the State will permanently lose the ability to 
USCA11 Case: 26-11705 Document: 7-2 Date Filed: 05/15/2026 Page: 4 of 7 
7a

- 5- 
exercise the Commission’s pre-election functions to keep the voting public 
informed about potential violations of the Code of Judicial Conduct. By 
election day, the campaign will be over, votes will have been cast, and 
any later action by the Committee will come too late to inform voters before they vote. 
13. Any public statement issued by the Special Committee after 
the election would not reach voters in time to serve its intended purpose. 
The Committee’s entire reason for existence is to deal expeditiously with 
allegations of ethical misconduct in campaigns for judicial office so that 
voters can be informed before they vote. Once the election has passed, 
that vital function becomes moot as to this election cycle.
14. The District Court’s injunction prevents the Commission from 
carrying out its core pre-election functions. Specifically, the injunction
halts the Special Committee’s ongoing process related to address the allegations contained in the complaints against Jordan and Rankin. As a 
result, the Commission is unable to exercise its constitutionally established authority to investigate campaign misconduct allegations and, if 
warranted, inform voters before they cast their ballots.
USCA11 Case: 26-11705 Document: 7-2 Date Filed: 05/15/2026 Page: 5 of 7 
8a

- 6- 
15. Even if the Special Committee determines after further investigation that the allegations warrant speedy intervention, the most the 
Special Committee can do during the election period is release a non-confidential public statement setting out the violations reasonably believed 
to exist and/or refer the matter to the full Investigative Panel. That statement is not a conclusive determination that the candidate’s conduct violated the Code of Judicial Conduct and does not require the candidate to 
change their speech or campaign behavior.

III. The balance of equities and the public interest weigh against injunctive relief.
Finally, Jordan and Rankin have not shown that the balance of equities or the public 
interest favors enjoining the Commission’s nascent proceeding. Because Plaintiffs sued 
Defendants in their official capacities, their suit is against the State of Georgia and these 
two factors “merge.” Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 435 (2009). Georgia and its citizens 
will suffer grave harm if the Commission is prohibited from continuing its administrative 
investigation process. Judicial “codes of conduct serve to maintain the integrity of the judiciary and the rule of law,” and these codes are “the principal safeguard against judicial
campaign abuses that threaten to imperil public confidence in the fairness and integrity of 
the nation’s elected judges.” Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co., 556 U.S. 868, 889 (2009)
(internal quotation marks omitted). Georgia thus has a weighty interest in investigating 
alleged violations of its Judicial Code. Williams-Yulee, 575 U.S. at 446. The First Amendment does not foreclose Georgia’s citizens from establishing by law that “[j]udges are not 
politicians, even when they come to the bench by way of the ballot.” Id. at 437-38. “A State 
may assure its people that judges will apply the law without fear or favor.” Id.
Plaintiffs argue that the equities favor them because this is “their one shot at this 
election.” Mot. 32. Nothing in the Committee’s decision to merely “further investigat[e]” 
the allegations against Plaintiffs, Veal Decl., Exs. A & B, jeopardizes Plaintiffs’ opportunity to win this election. Moreover, it is not enough for the State merely to “enforce its 
ethics code in the future,” because equity would not favor an election won through violation 
of the judicial code of conduct. Contra Mot. 32.; see Pharm. Care Mgmt. Ass’n v. Tufte,

in the face of unsupported, bare assertions of harm). Only the Commission’s continued 
investigation can determine whether any violation has occurred before Plaintiffs take office 
(if elected). 
The same is true of Plaintiffs’ public interest argument. They argue that enjoining 
the Commission’sinvestigation serves the public interest by “ensur[ing] that voters … have 
more information about their choices, not less.” Mot. 32. But if that additional information 
is obtained through violations of the judicial code of conduct, it bypasses the “the principal

integrity of the judiciary and the rule of law.” Caperton, 556 U.S. at 889. The Commission’s investigation is the state’s designated means of ensuring that those safeguards serve 
their vital purpose. Moreover, “more information” surely includes knowing whether a candidate for judicial office has engaged in conduct that could be violative of the Code of 
Judicial Conduct. The public, especially voters, deserve to know if Plaintiffs’ conduct 
could subject them to the Commission’s scrutiny. Enjoining the 
investigation could mean that voters have less relevant information, not more. 
CONCLUSION
This Court should not take the extraordinary step of enjoining Georgia’s sovereign 
insistence on public confidence in an impartial judiciary. The motion for a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction should be denied.

THE COMMISSION
3. The Commission is charged by Georgia law with investigating and 
prosecuting violations of the Georgia Code of Judicial Conduct. 
4. The Commission’s Investigative Panel receives complaints about 
judges and judicial candidates. If the complaint raises a campaign-related concern 
during a general election year, the complaint is forwarded to the Special Committee 
on Judicial Election Campaign Intervention (the “Special Committee”). 
5. The Special Committee reviews the complaint and if the Committee 
determines speedy intervention or further investigation are necessary, sends a 
confidential notice to the judge or judicial candidate who is the subject of the 
complaint. The notice lays out the alleged violations of the Code of Judicial Conduct 
but does not represent any final findings of the Special Committee or the 
Commission. 
6. The Special Committee does not have an enforcement mechanism to 
require the judge or judicial candidate to take any action regarding the allegations 
contained in the confidential notice. 
7. The notice also requests a confidential written response from the judge 
or judicial candidate. If the Special Committee determines after review of the judge 
or judicial candidate’s written response that speedy intervention is necessary, it may 
release a public statement setting out the violations of the Code of Judicial Conduct

I. The plaintiffs have standing. 
The plaintiffs have alleged, under penalty of perjury, the precise injury 
that Wollschlaeger v. Governor of Florida, 848 F.3d 1293 (11th Cir. 2017) (en 
banc), recognizes: that, in response to the threat of further enforcement, they 
have refrained from campaign speech they would otherwise engage in.1
(Compl. ¶ 40.) The defendants’ contrary arguments—that the plaintiffs have 
not removed past speech, that Barrow compels denial, and that an 
investigation is not censorship—each rest on a misreading of Wollschlaeger or 
a misreading of Barrow itself.

C. The Special Committee’s “investigation, not censorship” 
framing misses the point of pre-enforcement standing. 
The defendants repeatedly say that no speech has been “censored.” 
(Resp. 9, 11, 12.) That misses the point. Wollschlaeger, Susan B. Anthony,
and Driehaus all establish that an actual sanction is not required; the 
credible threat of sanction, plus self-censorship in response, is enough. See
848 F.3d at 1304–05; 573 U.S. at 158. The Special Committee has identified 
specific campaign conduct, demanded a response under threat of further 
proceedings, and is empowered to refer the matter for sanctions ranging from 
public reprimand and censure to suspension and removal from office—or even 
a lifetime ban on judicial service. See Comm’n R. 6(B), 17(D), 29(B)(4). That is 
a credible threat as a matter of law. Cf. Wilson v. State Bar of Ga., 132 F.3d 
1422, 1428 (11th Cir. 1998) (chill exists “when the plaintiff is chilled from 
exercising her right to free expression or forgoes expression in order to avoid 
enforcement consequences”).

III. The plaintiffs’ claims are ripe. 
The defendants argue that the plaintiffs’ claims are not ripe because 
the Commission has not yet “applied” the Code. (Resp. 17.) That is wrong 
factually and as a matter of law. 
It is wrong factually because the Commission has applied the rules. 
The Special Committee has identified specific campaign conduct—the joint 
commercial, the joint appearances, the third-party endorsements, four 
enumerated statements—and matched each item to specific rule provisions. 
The notice letters tell the plaintiffs that their conduct may “have violated” 
specific rules and demand a response under threat of further proceedings. 
(Compl. Exs. 1, 2.) That is application. 
It is wrong legally because in pre-enforcement First Amendment cases 
involving a credible threat of prosecution, ripeness and standing “boil down to 
the same question.” Wollschlaeger, 848 F.3d at 1304. The plaintiffs’ 
demonstrated self-censorship satisfies both. The defendants’ real position is 
that the plaintiffs must wait until either a public statement issues or formal 
charges are filed. But by then Younger would foreclose federal review under 
the defendants’ own theory of Younger, and the election will likely be over. 
The ripeness doctrine does not require waiting for an injury to become 
irreparable.

textualism is “telling voters what she will do” in textualism cases; a 
candidate who says she favors strong consumer protection is “telling voters 
what she will do” in consumer cases. Under the defendants’ theory, every 
White-protected statement on “disputed legal or political issues,” Republican 
Party of Minn. v. White, 536 U.S. 765, 770 (2002), becomes a forbidden 
commitment. That cannot be right and is not what the rule means. 
The defendants’ third-party endorsement theory is even more 
troubling. They argue that touting an endorsement from Reproductive 
Freedom for All “may constitute an implicit commitment.” (Resp. 25.) Their 
reasoning is that “when a candidate actively touts an endorsement from an 
organization whose stated mission is to ‘Fight for Reproductive Freedom’ … a 
future litigant may reasonably doubt that judge’s impartiality.” (Id.) That

that. See R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul, 505 U.S. 377, 391 (1992).
D. Rule 4.2(A)(3): The defendants do not allege a single false

The defendants concede that Rule 4.2(A)(3) requires “knowledge” or 
“reckless disregard” of falsity. (Resp. 26–27.) The notice letters do not allege 
that the plaintiffs made any specific statement that is false, let alone that 
any statement was made with knowledge or reckless disregard. The 
defendants make no such allegation in their brief either. (Resp. 27 (insisting 
only that the letters “specifically identify four categories of conduct and quote 
the specific statements at issue”)). Application of an actual-malice rule to 
speech the State concedes was not made with actual malice—and that the 
State does not contend was even false—cannot survive Weaver, 309 F.3d at 
1319.
V. The remaining injunction factors favor the plaintiffs. 
A. Irreparable Harm
The defendants concede that “the unconstitutional abridgement of 
speech can be irreparable harm.” Resp. 28 (citing KH Outdoor, LLC v. City of 
Trussville, 458 F.3d 1261, 1272 (11th Cir. 2006)). They argue only that no 
abridgement has occurred. That argument fails for the same reasons stated

enforcement remains in place is another day the plaintiffs cannot 
communicate freely with voters during early voting, which began April 27 in 
this election. (Resp. 3.) As Weaver recognized, there is no adequate postelection remedy for an unconstitutional restraint on judicial campaign 
speech. 309 F.3d at 1325. 
B. Balance of Equities 
The defendants argue that Georgia’s interest in continuing this 
particular investigation outweighs the plaintiffs’ interest in speaking. (Resp. 
29–30.) The balance is the other way. The plaintiffs face an imminent and 
irreversible election. The State’s investigation can resume after the election if 
the plaintiffs prevail and the rules are upheld. The State has no equivalent 
stake in this particular investigation continuing during the election. The 
defendants’ suggestion that an election “won through violation of the judicial 
code of conduct” would be tainted presupposes the very violations they have 
not established and assumes away the plaintiffs’ constitutional defenses. 
(Resp. 30.)

C. Public Interest 
The defendants do not seriously contest that vindicating First 
Amendment rights serves the public interest. See Scott v. Roberts, 612 F.3d 
1279, 1297 (11th Cir. 2010); Honeyfund.com Inc. v. Governor, 94 F.4th 1272, 
1283 (11th Cir. 2024). Their argument that the public has an interest in 
knowing whether the plaintiffs may have violated the Code (Resp. 30) 
collapses into the same point they make on irreparable harm and balance of 
equities, and it fails for the same reason. The Special Committee can pursue 
any legitimate state interest in judicial integrity through any number of 
mechanisms that do not require chilling the plaintiffs’ campaign speech in 
the closing days of an election. 
VI. Conclusion 
For these reasons and those stated in the plaintiffs’ motion, the Court 
should grant the requested temporary restraining order and preliminary 
injunction.

commercials, which circulated on television and social media, is a joint campaign 
advertisement with Jennifer Auer Jordan, also a candidate in a nonpartisan 
judicial election for a seat on the Supreme Court of Georgia. As the candidates 
appear together, Ms. Jordan informs viewers, “we’re running for Georgia 
Supreme Court to fight for what’s fair.” Each candidate makes additional
